detail.question: What does Mill claim about the abilities of women who have ruled as queens or regents?
detail.answer:
Mill claims that women who have ruled have shown real and often outstanding ability for government. His main points, as the passages give them:

1. Reigning queens are far fewer than kings, but a much larger proportion of them have shown talent for rule, even though many held the throne in difficult periods. They were often noted for firmness and vigour as well as intelligence, which are qualities opposite to the "imaginary and conventional character of women." Adding regents and viceroys of provinces makes the list of eminent women rulers very long (Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 5 (edition-specific)).

2. He rejects the quip that under kings women govern and under queens men govern. He cites French kings who gave direction of affairs to a mother and a sister, and Charles V's female Governors of the Netherlands, including Margaret of Austria, who ruled very successfully (Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)). Even if a queen is served by able men, Mill argues this shows her superior capacity for choosing them. He says most great queens were great by their own talents and kept supreme direction of affairs in their own hands (Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)).

3. In a note, he says that in India, from his official knowledge, a well-governed Hindoo principality is, in three cases out of four, under a woman's rule. He says he found this fact unexpected. These women act as legal regents during a male heir's minority, despite having been secluded and uneducated in politics. He calls this a very striking example of women's natural capacity for government (Mill, The Subjection of Women, Note footnote_2_1 to Chapter 3, paragraph 5 (edition-specific)).

4. He explains that princesses were not taught that politics was improper for them and were allowed the same range of interests as men. In their case no inferiority is found: wherever women's capacities for government have been tried, they have been found adequate in proportion (Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)).

5. He also says it is certain that a woman can be a Queen Elizabeth, a Deborah, or a Joan of Arc, because "this is not inference, but fact" (Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
On the passages provided, Kant gives the understanding the role of supplying unity to combinations of representations. Its role differs somewhat depending on which kind of combining is in view.

1. The understanding is the faculty of conjoining. It is "nothing more than the faculty of conjoining à priori and of bringing the variety of given representations under the unity of apperception." Combination is not simply taken up through perception but is "an operation of the understanding itself" (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 2, §12, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). Kant calls the synthetical unity of apperception the highest point to which every operation of the understanding must be connected, and says this faculty "is the understanding itself" (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Note block 155 to Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 2, §12, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

2. In judgement, it arranges representations under higher ones. Conceptions rest on functions, meaning "the unity of the act of arranging diverse representations under one common representation." The understanding can use conceptions only to judge. Judgements are therefore "functions of unity in our representations" (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 1, §4, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

3. In intuition, it gives unity to synthesis. The imagination performs the synthesis of the manifold (the diversity) of pure intuition. By itself this gives no cognition. The conceptions that give unity to this pure synthesis are supplied by the understanding, and they are the third requisite for cognition of an object (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 1, §6, paragraph 5 (edition-specific)). Kant also says the same function that unifies representations in a judgement unifies the synthesis of representations in an intuition. This unity is the pure conception of the understanding, and it applies à priori to objects (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 1, §6, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)). A related passage puts the division of labour this way: the synthesis of representations rests upon the imagination, while their synthetical unity rests upon the unity of apperception (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Book II, Chapter 2, Section II, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

4. It depends on unity of consciousness. Every union of representations requires unity of consciousness in their synthesis. That unity is what makes it possible for representations to relate to an object and become cognitions (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 2, §13, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

In short, the imagination does the synthesizing, and the understanding supplies the unifying conceptions and functions and is bound up with the unity of apperception. The passages do not spell out in more detail how the two faculties interact.

detail.question: What criticism does Hume make of philosophers who claim that all power belongs directly to God?

top_retrieved.author: Immanuel Kant
top_retrieved.locator: Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 35 (edition-specific)

detail.answer: Hume says these philosophers defeat their own purpose. They hold that mind is "the immediate and sole cause of every event which appears in nature," so that what we call causes are only occasions for God's volitions (Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VII, Part I, §55, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). Hume says they "rob nature, and all created beings, of every power" in order to make their dependence on God more immediate. But he argues that this theory diminishes, rather than magnifies, the grandeur of the divine attributes they want to celebrate (Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VII, Part I, §56, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). His reasons are that it shows more power in the Deity to delegate some power to inferior creatures than to produce everything by his own immediate volition. It also shows more wisdom to design the world from the start with such foresight that it serves providence by its own operation than to have the Creator adjust its parts at every moment (Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VII, Part I, §56, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer: Wollstonecraft says children should not be taught to make allowances for their parents' faults. She argues that every such allowance weakens the force of reason in their minds and makes them more indulgent to their own faults (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 11, paragraph 18 (edition-specific)). She treats this as a dilemma for the instructor: teaching virtue on any solid principle amounts to teaching children to despise their parents (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 11, paragraph 18 (edition-specific)). She distinguishes children from adults. Being severe with oneself and forbearing toward others is, she says, one of the most sublime virtues of maturity, but children should be taught only the simple virtues. If they start too early to make allowance for human passions and manners, they wear off the fine edge of the criterion by which they should regulate their own conduct, and become unjust in proportion as they grow indulgent (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 11, paragraph 18 (edition-specific)). The passages provided do not resolve how an instructor should handle this dilemma. Elsewhere she also criticizes blind submission to parents, saying it weakens the faculties, and that duty should rest on knowledge rather than mere authority (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 11, paragraph 13 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer: Hobbes lists four abuses of speech that correspond to the proper uses of language. The first is the one by which people deceive themselves: they register their thoughts wrongly because the signification (meaning) of their words is inconstant (unsteady). As a result they record as their conceptions something they never actually conceived (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 4, Abuses Of Speech, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). By contrast, Hobbes says the second abuse, using words metaphorically (in a sense other than the one they are ordained for), deceives others rather than oneself (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 4, Abuses Of Speech, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). Hobbes also warns that judging the nature of things by the ordinary and inconstant use of words is fallacious. He illustrates this with the confusion of counsel and command, since both use the imperative "Doe this" (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 25, Counsell What, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). The passages do not say whether this is the only way people deceive themselves with language. They name this as the first of four abuses.

detail.answer:
Wollstonecraft attacks these arguments on several grounds.

1. She says they do not follow logically. Even if woman were naturally weaker than man, it would not follow that she should labour to become weaker still. She calls such arguments "an insult to common sense" and says they "savour of passion". She compares the "DIVINE RIGHT" of husbands to the divine right of kings and hopes it can be contested without danger (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 3, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)).

2. She reports the opposing position. It holds that women should be weak and passive because they have less bodily strength, and that they are formed to please and be subject to man, with their duty being to make themselves agreeable to their "master" (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 5, §1, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). She also quotes a writer who says a woman should learn early to suffer injustice and to bear her husband's insults without complaint (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 5, §1, paragraph 21 (edition-specific)). She presents these as claims to be refuted, not as conclusions she accepts.

3. She argues that weakness makes women worse at the very duties they are meant to perform. Those who want to domesticate women try to weaken their bodies and cramp their minds. Yet family life and the education of children require understanding and strength of body and mind. She concludes that reason is necessary for a woman to perform any duty properly, and that "sensibility is not reason" (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 4, paragraph 45 (edition-specific)). She also questions whether passive, indolent women make the best wives. She asks whether women with notions of passive obedience have enough character to manage a family or educate children (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 2, paragraph 62 (edition-specific)).

4. She compares enforced subjection to tyranny. Tyrants are eager to crush reason while claiming to be useful, and she says a duty cannot be binding unless it is founded on reason. She argues that women's attachment to duty grows with understanding, and that no authority can make them discharge it virtuously unless they comprehend it. Otherwise they may be "convenient slaves", but slavery degrades both master and dependent (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Dedication, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)).

5. She links duties to rights. Without rights there cannot be incumbent duties. Women are made slaves to their persons and driven to govern their tyrants by "sinister tricks". She adds that the laws treat a man and his wife as one unit and consider only him responsible, which reduces her to "a mere cypher" (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 9, paragraph 15 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer: Wollstonecraft separates the two by whether a reason can be given for the belief. She says a prejudice is "a fond obstinate persuasion, for which we can give no reason". As soon as a reason can be given for an opinion, it stops being a prejudice, even if it may still be "an error in judgment" (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 5, §5, paragraph 28 (edition-specific)). So the difference lies in whether the belief rests on a traceable reason, not in whether it is true. She adds that opinions were probably all founded on some reason at first, though sometimes only a local expedient rather than a lasting principle. They turn into prejudices when they are "indolently adopted" only because age gives them a venerable aspect, while their original reason has ceased to hold or "cannot be traced" (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 5, §5, paragraph 28 (edition-specific)). She also observes that men often use their reason to justify prejudices they have absorbed, "they cannot trace how", instead of rooting them out. She contrasts this with the strength of mind needed to form one's own principles (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 1, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)). In a note she remarks that an ignorant person cannot be reasoned out of an error, and that being persuaded to swap one prejudice for another leaves the mind unsettled (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Note block 46 to Chapter 5, §1, paragraph 37 (edition-specific)). The passages do not give a fuller test for when a reason counts as adequate.

detail.answer:
Smith says that when great landowners spend their rents on tenants and retainers (household followers), each landlord maintains all of his own tenants and retainers entirely (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book III, Chapter 4, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)). When they spend on tradesmen and artificers, all of them together may maintain as many people as before, or even more, because rustic hospitality involves waste. Taken singly, though, each landlord contributes only a very small share to the maintenance of any one individual (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book III, Chapter 4, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)). A tradesman draws his living from a hundred or a thousand customers, so he is somewhat obliged to them all but not absolutely dependent on any one (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book III, Chapter 4, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).

By contrast, tenants and retainers are dependent on the proprietor. A tenant at will is as dependent as any servant or retainer, and the subsistence of both comes from the landlord's bounty and lasts at his pleasure (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book III, Chapter 4, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)). Smith also says that the older method of spending meant sharing with at least 1000 people, whereas spending on a luxury such as diamond buckles shared nothing with anyone (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book III, Chapter 4, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
The question's premise does not match the passages: Kant does not argue that scepticism gives definitive answers to the problems of reason. He says the opposite. In the Doctrine of Method he states that the sceptical procedure "does not present any solution of the problems of reason". Instead he calls it an exercise that awakens reason's circumspection and shows how it can establish its legitimate claims (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 37 (edition-specific)). He also says that, in itself, scepticism gives no certain information about the bounds of our knowledge. For that reason its investigations cannot settle the dispute over the rights and powers of human reason (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 31 (edition-specific)).

What scepticism does offer is limited. It is the second step in reason's development, after dogmatism and before criticism, which alone fixes the necessary limits of knowledge. Scepticism is "a resting place for reason" and not its permanent dwelling (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 28 (edition-specific)). Its polemic is aimed at the dogmatist, to expose the futility of his designs (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 31 (edition-specific)). Kant also calls the sceptical mode of treating reason's questions useful: it rids us of the confusions of dogmatism and puts a temperate criticism in their place (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Book II, Chapter 2, Section V, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He adds that this sceptical method is peculiar to transcendental philosophy (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Book II, Chapter 2, Section II, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)).

Kant criticizes the sceptic he discusses for failing to give definite answers. This thinker merely declared the understanding limited, without showing what its limits were (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 34 (edition-specific)). Kant also denies that doubt about dogmatic philosophy means reason cannot build a sound philosophy. After a thorough critical investigation, reason is bound either to establish the validity of its ideas or to expose their illusory nature (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 30 (edition-specific)). In these passages, then, any definitive answer comes from criticism and not from scepticism.

detail.question: How does Hume explain the occurrence of unexpected outcomes in the human body?

top_retrieved.author: Immanuel Kant
top_retrieved.locator: Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 27 (edition-specific)

detail.answer: Hume says that unexpected outcomes in the body do not show that its underlying principles are irregular. When the usual symptoms of health or sickness disappoint our expectation, or medicines fail to work with their usual powers, the philosopher and physician are not surprised. They do not deny the necessity and uniformity of the principles governing the animal economy (the workings of the body) (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VIII, Part I, §67, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). His explanation is that the human body is a very complicated machine. Many secret powers lurk in it that are beyond our comprehension, so to us its operations must often seem uncertain (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VIII, Part I, §67, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). The irregular events that show themselves outwardly therefore prove nothing against the laws of nature. Those laws may be observed with the greatest regularity in the body's internal operations (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VIII, Part I, §67, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). Hume applies the same reasoning to human actions. detail.answer:
Locke says power, as he is considering it, is two-fold: it is either able to make a change or able to receive a change. The first he calls ACTIVE power and the second PASSIVE power (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §2, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). He leaves open, as "worth consideration", whether matter lacks active power altogether, and whether created spirits alone can have both kinds. He says he will not pursue this, since his business is how we come by the idea of power, not its origin (same passage).

Locke adds that sensible things give us many ideas of passive power, because their qualities are in continual flux. Active power is the more proper sense of the word "power". Whenever we observe a change, the mind must collect a power somewhere able to make it, as well as a possibility in the thing to receive it (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §4, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). Bodies give us only an obscure idea of active power. A moving ball merely transfers motion and does not produce it, so its motion is "rather a passion than an action". Our clearer idea of active power comes from reflection on the operations of our own minds (same passage). Locke also points us to God and spirits for the clearest idea of active power (Locke, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §2, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

A related distinction appears in Chapter 22. The efficacy by which something new is produced is called ACTION in the subject exerting the power, but PASSION in the subject in which an idea is changed or produced (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 22, §11, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer: The passages do not support the claim in the question. Mill does not say that people always think only of their own pain when their sense of justice is violated. He takes up the objection that, when our sentiment of justice is outraged, we think only of the individual case and not of society. He says this is no objection to his doctrine (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 22 (edition-specific)). He grants that it is common, though not commendable, to resent something merely because we have suffered pain. But he says a person whose resentment is a real moral feeling first considers whether the act is blameable. Even if that person does not say so to himself, he feels he is asserting a rule that benefits others as well as himself (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 22 (edition-specific)). If someone regards the act solely as it affects him individually, Mill says he is not consciously just (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 22 (edition-specific)). Mill explains the pull toward self-focus this way: the natural feeling of retaliation, taken alone, tends to make us resent indiscriminately whatever is disagreeable to us. When it is moralized by the social feeling, it acts only in directions conforming to the general good (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 21 (edition-specific)). In his recapitulation, the sentiment of justice is the animal desire to repel or retaliate a hurt to oneself, widened by enlarged sympathy to include all persons (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 23 (edition-specific)). So the self-focused element is real, but Mill treats it as one component and not as the whole of the sentiment.

detail.answer:
Kant says we actually possess a priori synthetic cognitions, and he treats the principles of the understanding as proof of this: they "anticipate experience" (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 30 (edition-specific)). Someone who cannot grasp how these principles are possible might doubt whether they are really a priori. But he cannot declare them impossible or call the steps reason has taken under their guidance null (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 30 (edition-specific)). Kant allows that doubt about dogmatic philosophy, which proceeds without criticism, is well grounded. Even so, we cannot deny reason the ability to build a sound philosophy once a thorough critical investigation has prepared the way (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 30 (edition-specific)).

On reason's responsibility, Kant argues that the conceptions and questions produced by pure reason lie in the sphere of reason itself, not of experience. Reason must therefore settle them and show them to be either valid or inadmissible. We may not decline these problems by appealing to the nature of things or to the limits of human faculties, because reason is the sole creator of these ideas. It is therefore bound either to establish their validity or to expose their illusory nature (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 30 (edition-specific)).

A related point from another passage is that pure a priori conceptions cannot be justified by tracing them to experience. Experience may supply the occasioning causes of their production, but a deduction of the pure a priori conceptions can only be transcendental, never empirical (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 2, §9, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer: Hume judges Cartesian universal doubt to be ineffective as a route to certainty. He describes it as a scepticism that comes before all study and is recommended as a "sovereign preservative against error and precipitate judgement". It asks us to doubt all our former opinions and principles, and even our faculties. We are then supposed to re-establish the faculties' trustworthiness by a chain of reasoning from some original principle that cannot be fallacious (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section XII, Part I, §116, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). Hume offers two objections. First, no such original principle has a prerogative above other self-evident and convincing principles. Second, even if there were one, we could not advance a step beyond it except by using the very faculties we were supposed to distrust (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section XII, Part I, §116, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). He concludes that the Cartesian doubt, if a human being could ever actually reach it (he says plainly we cannot), would be entirely incurable. No reasoning could then bring us to assurance and conviction on any subject (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section XII, Part I, §116, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). The passages say nothing further about whether Hume thinks any other form of doubt achieves certainty.

detail.answer: Hobbes says the words Just and Unjust mean one thing when applied to men and another when applied to actions. Applied to men, they signify the conformity or inconformity of manners (one's manner of life) to reason. Applied to actions, they signify conformity or inconformity to reason of particular actions only (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Men, And Justice Of Actions What, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)). A just man is one who takes all the care he can that his actions be just, and an unjust man is one who neglects this. Such men are more often called Righteous and Unrighteous, though the meaning is the same (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Men, And Justice Of Actions What, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)). Because the two kinds of justice differ, a righteous man does not lose that title through one or a few unjust actions that come from sudden passion or a mistake about things or persons. An unrighteous man does not lose his character through actions he does, or refrains from doing, out of fear, because his will is shaped by the apparent benefit of what he is to do and not by justice (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Men, And Justice Of Actions What, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)). The justice of manners is the one meant when justice is called a Vertue and injustice a Vice (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Men, And Justice Of Actions What, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Burke suggests his countrymen should hold up the British Constitution as an example to the French, rather than take French models for improving their own. He calls the Constitution "an invaluable treasure" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 417 (edition-specific)).

He credits the nation's happy situation to the whole Constitution, not to any single part. In his view it owes much to what was left standing in earlier reviews and reformations, as well as to what was altered or added (same passage, paragraph 417). He says the people will find enough to occupy a patriotic, free and independent spirit in guarding what they possess from violation (paragraph 417).

He does not rule out alteration. But even when he changed something, it should be in order to preserve. A great grievance should lead him to his remedy, and he would follow the example of the ancestors, repairing as nearly as possible in the style of the building (paragraph 417). He urges imitating the cautious ancestors, who acted from a sense of the ignorance and fallibility of mankind. His words are: "Let us add, if we please, but let us preserve what they have left". Standing on the Constitution, they should be content to admire rather than follow the "aëronauts of France" in their desperate flights (paragraph 417).

Burke also wants his countrymen to return to the true principles of their own domestic laws and keep cherishing them. He sets this against a spreading spirit of change and contempt for ancient institutions (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 46 (edition-specific)). He warns that neither side should be imposed upon by counterfeit goods of "improved liberty" that are falsely presented as British (same passage, paragraph 46).

His objection to the French reforms is that the French had a government that could have been reformed rather than destroyed. He says they went through the destruction of their country to a bad constitution when they already had a good one (Edmund Burke, Substance of Speech on the Army Estimates, Volume III, paragraph 22 (edition-specific)). He adds that the instructions to the representatives in 1789 asked for reformation without any design to destroy the government (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 227 (edition-specific)).

detail.question: How does Mill distinguish between types of government interference in trade?
detail.answer:
Mill separates interferences with trade by whether they raise a question of liberty. First, he says trade is a social act, so restrictions on it fall within what society may control. He says free trade rests on grounds different from the liberty principle, though equally solid ones. Restraints on trade are still evils, but they are wrong only because they fail to produce the results intended (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). He adds that most questions about the limits of free trade are likewise not questions of liberty. His examples are preventing fraud by adulteration and enforcing sanitary precautions or protections for workers in dangerous jobs. Such controls are, in principle, undeniably legitimate (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

Second, some interferences with trade are essentially questions of liberty. These are cases where the aim is to make a particular commodity impossible or difficult to obtain, such as the Maine Law, the opium prohibition in China, and restrictions on selling poisons. Mill says these are objectionable as infringements on the buyer's liberty, not the seller's (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

Third, he sets aside a further class of questions where the reasons against interference do not turn on liberty. Here the issue is whether government should help people, doing something for their benefit rather than leaving it to individuals or voluntary combination (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 16 (edition-specific)). Objections to interference that does not infringe liberty may be of three kinds (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 17 (edition-specific)). The first is that the thing is likely to be better done by individuals than by government, since those personally interested are best fitted to conduct a business. This condemns the old interferences with the ordinary processes of industry (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 18 (edition-specific)). The passages provided do not state the other two kinds of objection.

detail.answer: Kant claims that using general logic as an organon (an instrument for producing knowledge) is a gross misuse, and that it yields only the appearance of knowledge. He explains that the mere form of a cognition, however well it fits logical laws, cannot supply material (objective) truth. So no one can use logic alone to say anything about objects or decide anything concerning them, unless he has already obtained well-grounded information about them independently of logic (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Logic, Introduction, Section III, paragraph 5 (edition-specific)). Because logic gives all our cognitions the form of the understanding, even when their content is deficient, it is tempting to treat it as a tool for the actual production, "or rather for the semblance of production," of objective assertions. Kant says this misapplies what is merely a canon of judgement (a standard for judging). General logic in this assumed role of organon is called dialectic (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Logic, Introduction, Section III, paragraph 5 (edition-specific)). This fits his wider view that logic is only a propædeutic, a preparatory vestibule of the sciences. It helps us judge correctly about branches of knowledge, but real, substantive knowledge must be sought in the objective sciences (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Preface to the Second Edition, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)).

He reasons that a paper circulation not backed by real money, forced in place of the kingdom's coin and becoming both its revenue and the medium of all commercial and civil dealings, "must put the whole of what power, authority, and influence is left" into the hands of the managers and conductors of the circulation (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 331 (edition-specific)).

The closest Burke comes to "equality" is a different point. He says the Assembly made the paper circulation compulsory in all payments in order to "put every individual on the same bottom" and bind the nation in "one guilty interest" to uphold the confiscation of Church property and the authority of those who did it. He says they used it to force even the most reluctant to share in the pillage (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 220 (edition-specific)). That describes a shared complicity, not an equal division of power. He also calls the compulsory paper currency a violent outrage upon credit, property, and liberty (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 221 (edition-specific)).

The Adam Smith passages do not address Burke's claim. They discuss the risks of paper money, not its effect on the distribution of power.

detail.question: According to Mill, should society always punish individuals for personal failings such as imprudence or lack of dignity?
detail.premise: Mill believes society should punish individuals for personal failings even when these do not harm others.
detail.answer:
No. Mill says that punishment is not the right response to purely personal failings. He sets out a maxim that the individual is not accountable to society for actions that concern only himself. In those cases, advice, instruction, persuasion and avoidance by others are the only justified ways for society to show its disapproval (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). He distinguishes the loss of consideration a person may rightly incur through lack of prudence or personal dignity from the reprobation due for an offence against others' rights. For the first, we may express distaste or keep our distance. We should not wish to punish him, and should instead try to alleviate his punishment by showing him how to avoid or cure the evils his conduct brings (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)). Mill states the opposing view: if society protects children, why not also adults who are unfit for self-government, and why not repress vices such as gambling, drunkenness or idleness (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 9 (edition-specific)). He answers that any merely contingent or constructive injury to society from conduct that breaks no specific duty and visibly hurts no one but the agent is an inconvenience society can afford to bear for the sake of human freedom (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)).

There are qualifications. When self-harming conduct leads someone to break a distinct obligation to others, such as failing to pay debts or support a family, he may be justly punished. But the punishment is for the breach of duty, not for the extravagance (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)). Drunkenness and idleness are ordinarily not fit subjects for legal punishment. Mill allows a special penalty for a person who has been violent to others when drunk, and compulsion where someone fails in legal duties such as supporting his children (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Smith describes the discovery of the American mines as lowering the value of gold and silver in Europe, though he is more confident about some points than others.

**Relative value (gold against silver).** Before the discovery, an ounce of fine gold was worth about 10 to 12 ounces of fine silver in the European mines. By the middle of the last century it was worth about 14 to 15 ounces. Gold therefore rose in nominal value, meaning the quantity of silver given for it (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 11, Part III, paragraph 91 (edition-specific)).

**Real value (labour and commodities).** Smith says both metals sank in real value, meaning the quantity of labour they could purchase, but silver sank more than gold. He explains this by saying that the silver mines of America seem to have been proportionally even more fertile than the gold ones (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 11, Part III, paragraph 91 (edition-specific)). His general principle is that when more abundant mines are discovered, more metal comes to market while the goods it must be exchanged for stay the same. Equal quantities of the metals must then be exchanged for smaller quantities of commodities (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 11, Part III, paragraph 40 (edition-specific)).

**Cause and timing.**
- Smith says the discovery of the abundant American mines seems to have been the sole cause of the fall in the value of silver relative to corn. He adds that supply had grown faster than demand, even though Europe was advancing in industry (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 11, Part III, paragraph 50 (edition-specific)).
- The effect on English prices was not very sensible until after 1570, although Potosi had been discovered over twenty years earlier (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 11, Part III, paragraph 50 (edition-specific)).
- Between 1630 and 1640, about 1636, the fall in silver's value relative to corn appears to have been completed. Silver seems to have risen somewhat afterwards, and probably began to rise even before the end of the last century (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 11, Part III, paragraph 53 (edition-specific)).
- Smith says the fall in the value of gold and silver was not owing to the growth of Europe's real wealth. It was due to the accidental discovery of more abundant mines than any known before (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 11, Part III, paragraph 144 (edition-specific)).

**Whether the decline continued.** Smith states that the discovery diminished the value of gold and silver in Europe (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 5, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)). Whether the fall was still going on is something he treats cautiously.
- In Book I, Chapter 5 he says it is commonly supposed to continue gradually, though he apprehends this is without any certain proof (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 5, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).
- In Book IV he says it is supposed, perhaps without much foundation, that over the present and preceding century the metals have been constantly but gradually sinking in value because of continual imports from the Spanish West Indies (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book IV, Chapter 1, paragraph 14 (edition-specific)).
- The later claim in Book I, Chapter 11, that the fall in silver was completed about 1636 and that silver then rose somewhat, sits uneasily with the idea of a continuing decline (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 11, Part III, paragraph 53 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer: Wollstonecraft sketches a sequence in which priests and chiefs first gain power, then monarchy and hierarchy emerge, and later rulers resort to covert corruption. (1) In the "infancy of society," when people were just emerging from barbarism, chiefs and priests had "unbounded sway" because they worked on hope and fear, which she calls the most powerful springs of savage conduct (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 1, paragraph 29 (edition-specific)). (2) She says aristocracy is "of course" the first form of government. Clashing interests then lose their balance, and a monarchy and hierarchy (priestly rule) break out of the confusion of ambitious struggles. The foundation of both is secured by feudal tenures, and she says this "appears to be" the origin of monarchial and priestly power and the dawn of civilization (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 1, paragraph 29 (edition-specific)). Her wording here is somewhat tentative: "appears to be." (3) She adds that such combustible materials cannot stay pent up. Foreign wars and internal insurrections give the people some power, which forces rulers to cover their oppression with a show of right. As wars, agriculture, commerce and literature expand the mind, despots must hold power through covert corruption rather than open force. Luxury and superstition spread this corruption most quickly (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 1, paragraph 29 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer: Smith says that restraints on importing foreign corn, though harmful in themselves, became necessary as a consequence of the bounty (a government payment to encourage exporting corn). detail.question: What does Locke argue about the relationship between conquest and the establishment of government?
detail.answer:
Locke argues that conquest is not a true beginning of government. Consent of the people is. He says governments can originally rise only from consent, and that people who count conquest as an origin have mistaken "the force of arms for the consent of the people" (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §175, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). His image is that conquest is as far from setting up a government as demolishing a house is from building a new one. Conquest may make way for a new frame of commonwealth by destroying the old one, but without the people's consent it can never erect a new one (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §175, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

Earlier, Locke had limited his historical claim to peaceful beginnings. He concludes that all of them were laid in the consent of the people. He sets conquest aside for later discussion, noting it is something "some esteem a way of beginning of governments" (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 8, §112, paragraph 22 (edition-specific)). He also says that governments begun in peace were made by the consent of the people (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 8, §104, paragraph 13 (edition-specific)).

Locke also limits what a conqueror gains. A conqueror gets no power over those who conquered alongside him. Using the Norman conquest of England as his example, Locke says the Normans who helped conquer and their descendants are freemen and not subjects by conquest (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §177, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). Damage suffered in a war does not let a conqueror dispossess the vanquished's posterity of their inheritance. If he claims to be master, that gives only the title that bare force gives to the stronger over the weaker (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §184, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)).

Even if a conqueror in a just war did have a right to the conquered's estates, which Locke says he plainly does not, nothing of absolute power would follow for the continuing government. The descendants are freemen, and what the conqueror grants them becomes their property, which cannot be taken without their own consent (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §193, paragraph 20 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer: Wollstonecraft recalls many women who were "not led by degrees to proper studies, and not permitted to choose for themselves." She says they were either "overgrown children" or, by mixing in the world, picked up a little of what is called common sense, meaning a way of seeing common occurrences as detached things. What deserves the name of intellect, the power of gaining general or abstract ideas, or even intermediate ones, was "out of the question" for them. Their minds were quiescent (inactive). When not roused by sensible objects and similar employments, they were low-spirited, would cry, or go to sleep (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 13, §2, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)). This follows her earlier account of one woman of fortune whose three daughters never saw a novel. They had masters who taught them the French and Italian names of furniture, and the few books they were given were beyond them or devotional. They "neither acquired ideas nor sentiments" and passed their time dressing, quarrelling, or talking secretly with maids until they were brought out as marriageable (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 13, §2, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)).

detail.question: According to Hume, what distinguishes belief from mere imagination or fiction?

top_retrieved.author: Immanuel Kant
top_retrieved.locator: Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section III, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)

detail.answer:
Hume holds that belief differs from fiction not in the ideas themselves but in how the mind feels and holds them.

1. The imagination is free to mix and recombine ideas, and it can picture invented events with every circumstance of time and place (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §39, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). Yet we cannot simply believe whatever we imagine. We can join a man's head to a horse's body, but we cannot believe such an animal ever existed (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §39, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

2. Belief is therefore not a special idea added to a conception. If it were, the mind could attach that idea to any fiction at will (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §39, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). Hume instead says the difference lies in a sentiment or feeling attached to belief and not to fiction. This feeling does not depend on the will and cannot be commanded at pleasure (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §39, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

3. The feeling arises from nature and custom. When an object is present to the memory or senses, custom carries the imagination to conceive the object usually conjoined with it. That conception is accompanied by a feeling different from the loose reveries of the fancy (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §39, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). Hume says we can conceive the contrary of any matter of fact. Without such a sentiment there would be no difference between a conception assented to and one rejected (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §39, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

4. Hume offers a description rather than a strict definition, and he admits that defining the feeling may be very difficult or impossible. He describes belief as a more vivid, lively, forcible, firm, steady conception of an object than the imagination alone can reach. He says belief consists in the manner of conception and its feeling to the mind, not in the nature or order of the ideas (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §40, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He says belief makes realities, or what is taken for such, weigh more in thought and gives them superior influence on the passions and imagination (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §40, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

5. In philosophy, Hume says, we can go no further than to assert that belief is something felt by the mind that distinguishes the ideas of the judgement from the fictions of the imagination. He adds that it makes these ideas more influential and the governing principle of our actions (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §40, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He sums up the doctrine by saying that belief is a conception more intense and steady than that of mere fictions. He says this arises from a customary conjunction of the object with something present to the memory or senses (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §40, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). He presents this summary as a supposition to be explored, not as a settled proof.

Kant says he simply asks himself a question: "Canst thou also will that thy maxim should be a universal law?" detail.answer: Smith says wages vary more between places than the price of provisions does. Provisions vary more from year to year, but wages vary more from place to place (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 8, paragraph 29 (edition-specific)). Bread and butchers' meat cost the same or nearly the same across most of the united kingdom. Most retail goods are as cheap or cheaper in great towns than in remoter parts. Yet wages in a great town and its neighbourhood are often a fourth or a fifth higher than a few miles away. His examples are London, at about eighteen pence a day against fourteen or fifteen pence nearby, and Edinburgh, at about tenpence against eightpence (same passage). He reasons that if labouring families can live where wages are lowest, they must be in affluence where wages are highest (same passage). He also says the variations in the price of labour do not correspond with those in the price of provisions, either in place or time, and are frequently quite opposite (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 8, paragraph 30 (edition-specific)). He qualifies this: provisions still influence wages. The money price of labour is regulated by the demand for labour and the price of necessaries and conveniencies of life. So money wages can be high where provisions are cheap, but would be higher still if provisions were dear and demand stayed the same (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 8, paragraph 50 (edition-specific)). For the very unequal wages found in nearby English places, he says the cause is probably the law of settlements. This law obstructs a poor man who would carry his industry from one parish to another without a certificate. He says such sudden differences between neighbouring places are not found in Scotland, and he believes not in other countries without settlement difficulties (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 10, Part II, paragraph 58 (edition-specific)). detail.answer:
Burke thinks the ministers' position is both perilous and degrading, for several reasons given in the passages.

1. The office has lost its dignity. In other countries the office of minister is of the highest dignity. In France Burke calls it "full of peril, and incapable of glory" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 350 (edition-specific)).

2. They are caught between two powers. Burke says they are "under two sovereigns, over neither of whom they have any influence." They lack confidence from the king, on whom they were forced, and from the Assembly, which forced them on him. As a result they must sometimes betray one, sometimes the other, and always themselves (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 353 (edition-specific)).

3. They have responsibility without power. Burke writes that they are "to execute, without power; they are to be responsible, without discretion; they are to deliberate, without choice." The noble functions of their office are carried out by committees of the Assembly, with no regard for the ministers' personal or official authority (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 353 (edition-specific)).

4. They are exposed to rivals and cannot properly defend themselves. Under the Constitution, their competitors can attack them in their vital parts, and the ministers can answer only in the degrading character of culprits. Burke adds that they are the only persons in France who cannot share in the national councils. He also says that responsibility prevents crimes but is a poor basis for active and zealous service (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 350 (edition-specific)).

5. They have had to witness the evils of the Revolution. Standing on an "eminence of humiliation," they must have seen and felt the degraded state of their country and their own utter incapacity of serving it. Burke says he would not have stood in their situation, and he is astonished that they have not already resigned (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 353 (edition-specific)). He also says their successors would be in the same situation (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 353 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
In the Epistle to the Reader, Locke says that someone who has "raised himself above the alms-basket" (that is, who no longer lives "lazily on scraps of begged opinions") and sets his own thoughts to work finding and following truth will not miss "the hunter's satisfaction" (Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, THE EPISTLE TO THE READER, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). Every moment of the pursuit rewards the effort with some delight. He can reasonably think his time well spent even when he cannot boast of any great acquisition (Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, THE EPISTLE TO THE READER, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). Locke also compares the understanding to the eye: it judges by its own sight and so is pleased with what it discovers, and it regrets less what has escaped it because that is unknown (same passage).

A related, more general remark appears in Book II. There Locke says that nobody is so senseless as to deny that there is pleasure in knowledge. He adds that this pleasure moves a person's desire only if he counts it part of his own happiness (Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §44, paragraph 45 (edition-specific)). That passage is about the pleasure of knowledge in general, not specifically about independent inquiry.

detail.answer:
Smith says the way French taxes are collected makes a large difference to how much of what is taken from the people actually reaches the crown. Most of the crown's revenue comes from eight sources: the taille, the capitation, the two vingtiemes, the gabelles, the aides, the traites, the domaine, and the farm of tobacco. The last five are, in most provinces, under "farm" (collection contracted out to private farmers). The first three are collected by an administration under the immediate direction of government. It is universally acknowledged, he says, that in proportion to what they take from the people, the government-run taxes bring more into the prince's treasury than the farmed ones, whose administration is much more wasteful and expensive (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 2, Part II, paragraph 205 (edition-specific)).

Smith's proposed reforms follow the same logic. Replacing the taille and capitation with more vingtiemes could preserve the crown's revenue while greatly lowering collection costs. Making the gabelle, aides, traites, tobacco taxes, customs and excises uniform across the kingdom would let them be levied at much less expense. The third reform he names is placing all these taxes under direct government administration; the passage breaks off before finishing that sentence (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 2, Part II, paragraph 206 (edition-specific)).

Smith also links the French system's poor yield to its overall design. The treasury received under 15 million pounds sterling, less than half of what he thought could be expected by comparison with Great Britain, even though the French people are generally acknowledged to be more oppressed by taxes (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 2, Part II, paragraph 207 (edition-specific)). His figures here come from accounts he admits are very imperfect.

On the capitation, the severe French government assesses a fixed sum on each generality (a tax district), which the intendant (the crown's provincial officer) must raise as he can. The intendant may overassess so that the overcharge on some covers the failure of others to pay. As a result the capitation always produces the expected sum, unlike the English poll-taxes (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 2, Part II, paragraph 126 (edition-specific)). This shows revenue being secured, but through a method Smith describes as severe, and which burdens the lower ranks.

The passages do not give precise cost-of-collection figures for each tax; they only state the comparison in general terms.

detail.question: Why does Locke argue that private property is never justified, even in the earliest societies?
detail.premise: Locke holds that private property is never justified, even in the earliest societies.

top_retrieved.author: Edmund Burke
top_retrieved.work: Reflections on the Revolution in France
top_retrieved.locator: Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 192 (edition-specific)

detail.answer:
The question's premise does not match the passages. Locke does not argue that private property is never justified, even in the earliest societies. In these passages he argues the opposite: property can arise legitimately, including in the first ages of the world.

Locke starts from the view that God gave the earth to mankind in common. He then sets out to show how men might come to have a property in parts of it, without any express compact of all the commoners (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §25, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

His answer is labour. Man is master of himself and proprietor of his own person and its labour, so he has in himself "the great foundation of property" (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §44, paragraph 23 (edition-specific)). Labour, in the beginning, gave a right of property wherever someone chose to employ it on what was common (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §45, paragraph 24 (edition-specific)). Locke gives examples. Game, fish and ambergris become the property of whoever bestows labour on them, even though they were previously common (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §30, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)).

Locke also argues that early appropriation was not unjust. The natural measure of property was the extent of a man's labour and his ability to enjoy what he took. So no one could encroach on another's right, because others still had room for as good and as large a possession (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §36, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).

Locke also treats the protection of property as a central purpose of society. Men join society for the mutual preservation of their lives, liberties and estates, which he calls by the general name "property" (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 9, §123, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). Within society, no one, including the supreme power, may take a man's property without his consent (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 11, §138, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)).

The passages therefore give no support for the claim that Locke thought private property is never justified.

detail.answer:
Mill says the reasons behind liberty of thought and expression are less familiar than one might expect. He notes that these liberties, to a considerable extent, already form part of the political morality of countries that profess religious toleration and free institutions. Even so, he says the philosophical and practical grounds on which they rest are "perhaps not so familiar to the general mind, nor so thoroughly appreciated by many even of the leaders of opinion, as might have been expected" (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 1, paragraph 16 (edition-specific)). His wording is tentative ("perhaps"). He adds that these grounds, rightly understood, apply much more widely than to this one branch of liberty. He also acknowledges that the subject has been discussed for about three centuries, and he asks the indulgence of readers to whom nothing he says will be new (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 1, paragraph 16 (edition-specific)).

By contrast, he treats one aspect as already well covered. This is the defence of the liberty of the press as a security against corrupt or tyrannical government. He says it has been so often and so triumphantly enforced by earlier writers that it need not be specially insisted on (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Locke says he is willing to revise his views on liberty and has done so. In Book II, Chapter 21, he says he gave an account of his thoughts on will, volition, liberty and necessity in an earlier edition, "according to the light I then had". Writing "as a lover of truth, and not a worshipper of my own doctrines", he admits "some change of my opinion". He says he followed truth with "unbiassed indifferency" the first time. He claims neither infallibility nor a wish to hide his mistakes to protect his reputation, and he is "not ashamed to publish what a severer inquiry has suggested" (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §74, paragraph 84 (edition-specific)). He adds that readers may prefer his former view, his later one, or neither, and that he would be beholden to anyone who could clear the subject of any remaining difficulties (same passage).

He explains how the revision came about. He had feared a mistake in the chapter himself, and a judicious friend suspected one without being able to point to it. This led him to a stricter review, in which he found a slip: he had put one seemingly indifferent word for another. That discovery gave him the new view he offers in the second edition (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §73, paragraph 83 (edition-specific)).

The Epistle to the Reader says the same. After closer inspection of men's minds, Locke found reason to alter his earlier thoughts about what finally determines the Will in voluntary actions. He says he acknowledges this freely, thinks himself more concerned to renounce an opinion of his own than to oppose another's when truth is against it, and seeks "truth alone". He qualifies this: the objections printed against his book have not given him light or reason to change his views on any of the questioned points. He suggests that readers may be prepossessed or that his expressions may be obscure, so his meaning is often mistaken (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, THE EPISTLE TO THE READER, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Kant describes reason, in its logical use, as the faculty of conclusion, or mediate (indirect) judgement. It works by subsuming (placing) the condition of a possible judgement under the condition of a given judgement (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Book I, Section II, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).

The steps of a syllogism are as follows:
- The given judgement is the general rule, the major. The subsumption of another possible judgement's condition under the rule's condition is the minor. The actual judgement that asserts the rule in the subsumed case is the conclusion (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Book I, Section II, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).
- Since the rule states something generally under a condition, and that condition is met in a particular case, what holds generally must also hold in the particular case (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Book I, Section II, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).
- In Kant's first-person account, he thinks the rule through the understanding (the major) and subsumes a cognition under the rule's condition through the judgement (the minor). He then determines the cognition by the rule's predicate, and so determines it à priori by reason (the conclusio) (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Introduction, Section II, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)).

Kant's example runs from "All compound is changeable" to "Bodies are compound" to "Consequently, bodies are changeable." He calls this reaching a cognition (the conclusion) through a series of conditions (the premisses) (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Book I, Section II, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)). Because such a series can be continued, the same procedure leads to a chain of syllogisms, extendable indefinitely toward either the conditions or the conditioned (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Book I, Section II, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).

The process can also be run in the other direction. Reason seeks the general condition of its conclusion, and the rule can itself be subjected to the same process. Kant says this shows reason's peculiar principle in its logical use is to find the unconditioned for the conditioned cognition of the understanding (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Introduction, Section II, paragraph 16 (edition-specific)). When the conclusion follows from a general rule, reason is also working to bring the variety of the understanding's cognitions under the smallest possible number of principles, in order to produce the highest unity (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Introduction, Section II, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).

Kant also distinguishes two employments of reason in deducing the particular from the general:
- Demonstrative or apodeictic employment: if the general is certain and given, the judgement need only subsume the particular under it, and the particular is thereby necessarily determined (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)).
- Hypothetical employment: if the general is only problematical (a mere idea), certain particular cases are examined to see whether the rule fits them. If all the cases that can be collected follow from it, its universality is inferred (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)).

detail.question: What does Kant say about the reality of the object associated with the idea of systematic unity?
detail.answer:
Kant says the object associated with the idea of systematic unity is a mere idea, not a thing assumed to be real in itself. Reason cannot think this unity without also thinking an object of the idea. That object cannot be presented in any experience and offers no concrete example of complete systematic unity. He calls it "a mere idea" that is "not assumed to be a thing which is real absolutely and in itself" (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 46 (edition-specific)). It serves only as the "problematical foundation" of the connection the mind introduces among phenomena. We view that connection as if it came from the supposed being corresponding to the idea, but the aim is only to have the idea as a secure foundation for the systematic unity of experience (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 46 (edition-specific)).

This fits his wider treatment of systematic unity. As a mere idea, it is a projected unity, to be regarded "only in the light of a problem" rather than as given (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 8 (edition-specific)). It is a subjective maxim, not an objective principle extending over objects. It is also objective only in an indefinite respect, and it is regulative, not constitutive, so it does not determine an object to which it directly relates (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 45 (edition-specific)). Kant also warns against hypostatizing the principle, meaning treating it as a real thing. He says this "perverted reason" error destroys the unity of nature, because it makes that unity foreign to the nature of things (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 54 (edition-specific)).

There is a qualification. Kant says that in relation to the criterion of empirical truth, we "must suppose" the idea of systematic unity to possess objective validity and necessity (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 13 (edition-specific)). He also says it is natural to assume a legislative reason corresponding to the idea (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 56 (edition-specific)). But this is a natural assumption, not a proof of that object's independent reality. The passages do not settle further how these points fit together.

Hobbes says the word Church (Greek Ecclesia) "signifieth in the Books of Holy Scripture divers things" (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, Church The Lords House, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). The meanings he lists are:

1. **God's House, a temple.** Hobbes says this use is uncommon ("though not often"). It is a place where Christians assemble for public holy duties, as in 1 Cor. 14:34. He calls this a metaphor for the congregation assembled there, which later came to name the building itself. The English word comes from the Greek Kuriake, "The Lord's House" (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, Church The Lords House, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

2. **A congregation or assembly of citizens.** When not taken for a house, Church means what Ecclesia meant in the Greek commonwealths: citizens called forth to hear the magistrate speak. If called by lawful authority it was a lawful church (Ecclesia Legitima). If stirred up by tumultuous and seditious clamor it was a confused church (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, Ecclesia Properly What, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

3. **Those with a right to be of the congregation, even if not assembled.** This means the whole multitude of Christians however dispersed, as in Acts 8:3, and it is the sense in which Christ is called Head of the Church (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, Ecclesia Properly What, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)).

4. **A certain part of Christians**, as in Col. 4:15, "Salute the Church that is in his house" (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, Ecclesia Properly What, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)).

5. **The Elect only**, as in Ephes. 5:27, which he says is meant of the Church Triumphant, or Church To Come (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, Ecclesia Properly What, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)).

6. **A congregation assembled of professors of Christianity**, whether their profession is true or counterfeit, as in Mat. 18:17 (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, Ecclesia Properly What, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)).

Hobbes adds that only in the last sense, a lawful congregation, can the Church be taken as one Person with power to will, command, and make laws. He defines a Church in that sense as "a company of men professing Christian Religion, united in the person of one Soveraign" (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, In What Sense The Church Is One Person Church Defined, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
The passages do not support the premise. Hobbes argues the opposite: the sovereign should regulate opinions and doctrines. He says it belongs to the sovereign power to judge which opinions and doctrines are harmful to peace and which help it (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 18, And Judge Of What Doctrines Are Fit To Be Taught Them, paragraph 9 (edition-specific)). His reason is that "the Actions of men proceed from their Opinions," so governing opinions well is how a sovereign governs actions well for the sake of peace and concord (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 18, And Judge Of What Doctrines Are Fit To Be Taught Them, paragraph 9 (edition-specific)). He also says the sovereign must judge or appoint all judges of opinions and doctrines, to prevent discord and civil war (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 18, And Judge Of What Doctrines Are Fit To Be Taught Them, paragraph 9 (edition-specific)).

Hobbes's related argument concerns private conscience. He calls private consciences "private opinions" and warns that if each person followed his own, the commonwealth would be distracted. No one would obey the sovereign further than it seemed good in his own eyes. For someone living in a commonwealth, he says, the law is the "publique Conscience" (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 29, Erroneous Conscience, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)).

The view that rulers should not control opinion appears in Mill, not Hobbes. Mill calls the power to coerce opinion illegitimate, even when a government acts in agreement with the people (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).
